ideas_for_vafer: Adopt: end each researcher reply with a calibration block (position, confidence, boundary conditions, what would change it, evidence weight), as in hooks.py:538-553. It cheaply feeds 'Where sources disagree'.
Adopt: resolve each disagreement explicitly (which side has the better evidence and the load-bearing reason) instead of listing both sides (step 7:54-58).
Adopt: a period-pinned check before drafting: a figure for 'Q3 2024' must come from the Q3 2024 record, not the latest one (step 8:31-58).
Adopt: when two researchers' facts conflict, open both cited pages and write a one-line verdict before writing (step 11:49-63). This maps onto VAFER's CONFLICT rows.
Adopt: the writing rules 'choose which sources to cite per point, never which points to make' and 'coverage and mechanism depth before elegance' (hooks.py:2278-2322, CHANGELOG.md:185).
Adopt: tell the writer to carry a researcher's developed mechanism (formula, decomposition, causal chain with numbers) into the report rather than compress it to a mention (hooks.py:2290-2297).
Adopt: a redundancy pass after VAFER's section-by-section writing, so each fact and caveat appears once (hooks.py:2331-2343).
Adopt: write-once after the final write, with one permitted compression pass triggered by a mechanical word count (step 11:226-243).
Adapt: score checklist items on importance, uncertainty and decision impact to set researcher count and depth, and record the allocation in plan.md (step 4:67-81).
Adapt: in heavy Deep runs, give the final write to a fresh writer subagent with a compact brief and the ability to open notes, not only drafts (step 11:18-20).
Adapt: for contested questions, replace three full drafts with one ~300-word 'strongest minority case' outline that the single writer must answer (step 10:84-87).
Adapt: run a pre-draft 'what would overturn this?' search on each headline conclusion, and log a miss as 'searched, not found (queries)', never as added confidence (step 8:117).
Avoid: three full drafts plus a merger by default. That is about three extra full Opus drafts per run with no ablation behind it (CHANGELOG.md:390).
Avoid: telling any agent to read 20-50 full documents. Keep 'load only that section's notes' and quotes of at most 30 words (hooks.py:1968-1971, cli/note.py:219-226).
Avoid: checking quotes against 'anywhere in the corpus'. Check each quote against the page it is cited to (cli/lint.py:110-148).
Avoid: mandatory steps enforced only by prose. Give every always-run VAFER step (gap-finder, re-opening headline sources) a checkable artifact (core/runs.py:808-842).
Avoid: promises between steps that no later step consumes, like step 7's 'mandatory Source Tensions section'. Name every promised section in the writer's instructions.
Avoid: one artifact described by several schemas (loci in step 4:83-102 vs hooks.py:264-289 vs hooks.py:396-398). Define each artifact once.
Avoid: judge-driven mandates (numbered headings, 80-150 citations, 5,000-10,000 words) unless VAFER explicitly decides to optimize for a benchmark judge. Make that decision up front.
Avoid on Windows: unquoted executable paths and bash-only env prefixes in instructions that may run under PowerShell (hooks.py:69, step 8:39).

key_claims.claim: No artifact from steps 5-11 is checked by the ship gate. The three drafts, synthesis plan, digest and source tensions are not checked anywhere in code; interim-note and comparisons checks exist only as lint rules outside the gate.
key_claims.where: src/hyperresearch/core/runs.py:649-844 (esp. 783-806, 808-842); src/hyperresearch/cli/lint.py:1005-1095, 1603-1624; grep 'draft-a' in cli/lint.py and core/runs.py returns nothing

key_claims.claim: The three drafts are not chosen among. A fresh Opus synthesizer limited to Read and Write rewrites the report from the drafts, the digest and an orchestrator-written plan, and only contradictions between drafts are checked against source text.

What depth investigates is decided entirely by LLM judgment in step 4: loci come from summaries plus contradiction clusters, four 0-10 scores are summed, and budget brackets are not enforced. The seed fields corpus_evidence and opposing_positions are dropped between producer and consumer.
Each of the three Opus drafters must read 20-50 notes in full through a command with no paging, which makes step 10 the dominant token cost and a truncation risk.

The triple draft's contribution to quality is unmeasured in the repo. Release 0.7.0 removed an earlier three-draft ensemble, V8 restored it on anecdote, and the only number is a 10-task benchmark score for the whole pipeline.

The ship gate's quote check accepts a quoted span found in any vault note body. LLM-written interim and source-analysis notes are indexed vault notes, so the check does not tie a quote to the source it is cited to.

acquisition.subsystem: Search providers, fetching, PDFs, open-access rescue and scholarly APIs (hyperresearch 0.12.0, HEAD 327498b)
acquisition.summary: hyperresearch splits acquisition between agent and Python. The orchestrator plans 40-100 searches and runs them with the host's WebSearch. `hpr scholar search` queries OpenAlex, Crossref, DOAB and ClinicalTrials.gov without keys, and CORE, EDGAR and FRED with a key or an email, then dedups by DOI and title. Python's six web providers (builtin, crawl4ai, exa, tavily, parallel, serply) act only as fetch backends in the pipeline. `provider.search()` is called only by `hpr research`, which the pipeline never uses. Ten to twelve Sonnet fetcher subagents run `hpr fetch` once per URL. Each call is a new process, and with crawl4ai (a hard dependency, made the default by `install`) it launches a fresh stealth headless Chromium. Python then extracts fit_markdown or PDF text (pymupdf, arXiv abs->pdf) and applies an SSRF gate plus substring junk and login-wall gates. It captures DOIs and swaps thin paywalled pages for an open-access copy from Unpaywall, Europe PMC or CORE, with a disclosure banner. Blocked pages are queued for a human Chrome lane. The fetcher then reads each full body, summarises it and extracts quoted claims. The full profile targets 55-80 sources in about 1.5-2.5 h.

mechanisms.name: Agent-side search plan and execution
mechanisms.what: The orchestrator writes a search plan with 3-4 lenses (breadth, citation depth, adversarial, period-pinned filings). It runs 40-100 searches with the host's WebSearch, removes exact-URL duplicates, gives each URL a 0-18 utility score, and splits the queue into batches of 8-12 URLs, one per fetcher.
mechanisms.why: It decides which sources exist in the corpus at all. The adversarial and period-pinned lenses add counter-evidence and primary filings.
mechanisms.cost: 40-100 WebSearch calls plus LLM scoring in the orchestrator's context (estimate).

mechanisms.name: Fetcher subagents (per-URL fetch, read, claims, chase)
mechanisms.what: 10-12 parallel Sonnet agents per wave. For each URL: sources check, hpr fetch, note show -j (full body), note update with summary and tags, then a claims-<id>.json of 3-25 claims with verbatim quotes. Phase 2 chases 3-8 cited primary sources, finding URLs with WebSearch and fetching them with --suggested-by.
mechanisms.why: The quoted claims feed the evidence digest. Chasing citations raises the share of primary sources.
mechanisms.cost: About 5-6 tool calls per URL, full page text in context (no cap: cli/note.py:221-227), roughly 1 min of wall time per URL (estimate).

mechanisms.name: crawl4ai stealth headless browser lane
mechanisms.what: Uses patchright's UndetectedAdapter and simulate_user. A DOM-stability smart-wait lasts 3-11 s, then PruningContentFilter produces fit_markdown, and a screenshot is taken on every fetch. TLS is verified with the cert-ignore flags stripped, and the final URL gets an SSRF recheck.
mechanisms.why: It reaches JavaScript-rendered and bot-shy pages, and returns cleaner main text than plain httpx.
mechanisms.cost: A fresh Chromium per `hpr fetch` (web/crawl4ai_provider.py:396). 10-12 browsers run at once. The screenshot is thrown away unless --save-assets is set.

mechanisms.name: builtin httpx lane
mechanisms.what: An SSRF-gated GET, then bs4 or stdlib HTML-to-text, with code blocks fenced so they cannot be read as wiki-links.
mechanisms.why: Fallback only. It cannot run JavaScript and sends the UA 'hyperresearch/0.1' (web/safe_http.py:41).
mechanisms.cost: Cheap, but many sites block it.

mechanisms.name: Search/fetch API providers (Exa, Tavily, Parallel, Serply)
mechanisms.what: Optional backends. Exa (neural search, EXA_API_KEY), Tavily (TAVILY_API_KEY, 'advanced' depth), Parallel (a keyless MCP endpoint at search.parallel.ai/mcp) and Serply (Google SERP, SERPLY_API_KEY).
mechanisms.why: The pipeline never calls their search, because the only caller is cli/research.py:62. As fetch backends, Exa and Serply cap content at 8,000 chars and skip the PDF lane.
mechanisms.cost: API keys and credits for Exa, Tavily and Serply; none for Parallel.

mechanisms.name: PDF lane
mechanisms.what: Detects PDFs by URL shape (.pdf, /pdf/, arXiv abs or pdf) or by %PDF- magic bytes. Rewrites arXiv /abs/ to /pdf/. Downloads with a Chrome UA, a 25 MB cap and verified TLS, extracts text with pymupdf get_text('text'), saves the raw PDF and records why a PDF failed.
mechanisms.why: It yields full papers instead of abstract pages. 87 of the 97 unique URLs cited in the example report are arXiv.
mechanisms.cost: Up to 25 MB per download, 30 s timeout. No OCR and no table structure.

mechanisms.name: SSRF gate, TLS policy and byte caps
mechanisms.what: Allows only http(s). Resolves the host and refuses private, loopback, link-local, multicast, reserved, unspecified, CGNAT, mapped and 6to4 addresses. Follows redirects by hand (at most 5), checking every hop. Streams the body under caps of 10 MB HTML, 25 MB PDF and 2 MB image. Never retries a refused certificate unverified.
mechanisms.why: It is a safety measure, not a quality one.
mechanisms.cost: An extra DNS lookup per hop and about 360 lines of code. DNS rebinding is an accepted risk (web/safe_http.py:16-21).

mechanisms.name: Junk and login-wall gates
mechanisms.what: Substring signal lists on the title and the first 500-2,000 chars of content: bot-wall, error-page, cookie-wall and login words, plus a binary-garbage ratio and a 300-char minimum. A rejected page goes to OA rescue, then escalation, then exit.
mechanisms.why: They keep CAPTCHA and error pages out of the corpus, but they also reject real pages (see weaknesses).
mechanisms.cost: Negligible CPU. The real cost is lost sources.

mechanisms.name: Escalation to a real-Chrome browser-fetcher
mechanisms.what: Blocked URLs (login wall, bot wall, CAPTCHA) with utility of at least 8, or no score, are queued, at most 25 per run. One browser-fetcher subagent drains the queue serially through Claude-in-Chrome, and CAPTCHAs, logins and 2FA go to the human.
mechanisms.why: It recovers walled sources that headless browsing cannot reach.
mechanisms.cost: Serial and needs the human. It does not exist on Codex, where queued items stay queued.

mechanisms.name: Open-access substitution (thin page with a DOI)
mechanisms.what: If a non-PDF result is under 6,000 chars or contains a paywall phrase, and a DOI was found, the candidates are tried in order: Unpaywall (only when [scholar] contact_email is set), Europe PMC JATS, then CORE (only with CORE_API_KEY). At most 3 attempts. The winner must pass the junk gate, be longer than the original and reach 6,000 chars.
mechanisms.why: For academic sources the vault holds the full text rather than an abstract. Out of the box only Europe PMC's biomedical OA subset is active.
mechanisms.cost: Up to 3 resolver lookups (cached for 30 days) plus up to 3 downloads or browser fetches per thin DOI page.

mechanisms.name: Open-access rescue (source unreadable)
mechanisms.what: After a fetch exception, a login wall or a junk verdict, the same resolvers are tried using a DOI from the URL or meta tags only. The resulting note is marked oa_recovery_kind: rescued.
mechanisms.why: It turns lost paywalled papers into notes, but only when a DOI can be found. After a hard failure that means a doi.org URL.
mechanisms.cost: Same as substitution.

mechanisms.name: Substitution disclosure
mechanisms.what: Puts a blockquote banner at the top of the body (substituted or rescued wording, version prose, licence, and a 'Quote this source with care' line when the copy is not the published version). Adds oa_* frontmatter, an oa block in note show -j, and CLI and JSON fields.
mechanisms.why: It stops preprints and accepted manuscripts from being quoted as the version of record.
mechanisms.cost: Tiny.

mechanisms.name: DOI and arXiv-id capture
mechanisms.what: Tries, in order: a DOI in a doi.org URL, an arXiv URL, a citation_doi or dc.identifier meta tag, then a 'DOI:' marker in the first 20,000 chars of the body.
mechanisms.why: Open-access lookup and citation enrichment both depend on it.
mechanisms.cost: Regex only.

mechanisms.name: Scholarly discovery registry and cross-provider dedup
mechanisms.what: `hpr scholar search` queries OpenAlex, Crossref, DOAB and ClinicalTrials.gov without keys, EDGAR with an email, CORE and FRED with keys, plus a RePEc stub that is always unavailable. Providers run one at a time. Records are merged by DOI, then by title fingerprint with year +/-1, taking the best value for each field.
mechanisms.why: It surfaces canonical papers, OA books, trials and filings, and its dedup keeps source counts honest.
mechanisms.cost: About 10-25 s per query (estimate; DOAB runs ~0.6 s per record, scholar/providers/doab.py:38-41). The output is large indent=2 JSON with full abstracts and author lists.

mechanisms.name: API cache and per-host courtesy throttle
mechanisms.what: An api_cache SQLite table holds successful bodies for 30 days. A per-host delay table spaces out uncached calls. Enrichment calls retry a 429 three times and honour Retry-After.
mechanisms.why: It saves cost and protects rate limits.
mechanisms.cost: The throttle state lives in a module-level dict, so it works per process only. Each CLI call starts fresh.

mechanisms.name: Citation enrichment, retraction sweep and authority percentile
mechanisms.what: For each DOI, OpenAlex (with Semantic Scholar as fallback) supplies citation count, venue and is_retracted. These go into the frontmatter and the DB. Authority is the vault-relative percentile of log1p(citations). `sources retractions` reruns the check fresh at ship time.
mechanisms.why: The retraction check is a ship gate, and authority is one input to quality_score.
mechanisms.cost: One API call per DOI, run serially.

mechanisms.name: Tier and content-type heuristics at fetch time
mechanisms.what: Guesses from URL and MIME type: any .gov domain is ground_truth, a PDF is a paper and institutional, forums are practitioner, news and blogs are commentary.
mechanisms.why: The result feeds quality_score (w_tier 0.35, core/config.py:115), but the guesses are coarse.
mechanisms.cost: Trivial.

mechanisms.name: Note write, source record, race handling and sync
mechanisms.what: Writes the note and raw file, syncs, records the source with INSERT OR IGNORE, reclaims orphaned rows, detects a lost race and cleans up.
mechanisms.why: Bookkeeping.
mechanisms.cost: Every CLI command auto-syncs, which globs and opens every note file.

mechanisms.name: Batch fetch (fetch-batch / fetch_many)
mechanisms.what: One browser serves the whole batch through arun_many. The command writes all notes, syncs once, then auto-links.
mechanisms.why: The pipeline's fetchers do not use it. It also skips the junk gate.
mechanisms.cost: It would save per-URL browser launches.

mechanisms.name: Untrusted-content wrapping
mechanisms.what: `note show` wraps fetched bodies in <untrusted-source> fences and neutralizes forged fence tags.
mechanisms.why: It defends against prompt injection rather than improving content.
mechanisms.cost: Tiny.

ideas_for_vafer: Adopt a keyless DOI-to-open-access recipe for cited papers: OpenAlex works/doi:<doi>?select=best_oa_location,is_retracted, then Europe PMC fullTextXML, then Unpaywall when the user supplies an email.
Prefer structured full text over PDF text: arXiv HTML (arxiv.org/html/<id>) and Europe PMC JATS. hyperresearch rewrites abs to pdf and loses structure.
State the version (preprint, accepted or published) next to every paper citation, and never quote a preprint as the version of record.
Run a ship-time retraction check on cited DOIs. It costs one OpenAlex call per DOI.
Avoid substring login and junk gates. Let the reading model judge each page, and record 'blocked: <reason>' with the URL in the notes.
Never replace a page's content with a paper found through a DOI in its body. Cite the paper as its own source.
Read DOIs from any URL path (/doi/10.x) and from citation_doi meta in either attribute order. When a publisher blocks, resolve the title to a DOI through Crossref or OpenAlex.
Canonicalize URLs before dedup and before counting sources: scheme, www, trailing slash, utm_* and fbclid parameters, fragments.
Count independent records, not URLs, so syndicated copies of one press release count once.
Keep scholarly API responses small: use select= fields, at most 10 per page, and skip abstracts unless needed. This avoids hyperresearch's indent=2 output blowup.
Query different API hosts in parallel. Per-host politeness does not require serializing across hosts.
Treat a 429 or 5xx from an API as 'unknown' and say so in the method note, never as 'no results'.
Do not pour whole pages into subagent context. Ask WebFetch targeted questions, and save full reads for the sources behind headline facts.
Do not spawn a browser per URL. Keep host WebFetch as the default, and use curl only for raw text or exact quotes.
Copy the period-pinned filing rule (fetch the filing for the named period and copy table line items verbatim) into VAFER's primary-record rule.
Give researchers the EDGAR full-text search URL template, noting that it returns 403 without a User-Agent that carries a contact email.
List blocked URLs and their reasons in the report's 'Not established' section, not in a hidden queue.
Keep prompt commands shell-neutral. A 'VAR=x cmd' prefix breaks under PowerShell in Codex on Windows.
For large reports, look for HTML or per-chapter versions. hyperresearch drops PDFs over 25 MB.
Beat it on time and cost: hyperresearch spends about 1.5-2.5 h and hundreds of tool calls for 55-80 sources, while VAFER Standard can reach the primary records with far fewer opens.
Avoid provider sprawl: hyperresearch ships six web providers but its pipeline uses only the fetch side of one. Rely on host search and document the fallbacks.

pipeline-front.subsystem: Entry router, tiers and the first research steps (1-4)
pipeline-front.summary: hyperresearch's front half is a long prompt pipeline over a small Python CLI. A bootstrap skill installs Jinja-rendered skills and agents. The router skill loads one step skill at a time (to survive context compaction), tracks its position in TodoWrite plus a run manifest, and routes by a tier that step 1 picks: light runs steps 1, 2, 10, 15 and 16; full runs all 16 plus 14.5; dissertation is an experimental chapter loop. Scale numbers come from an install-time gear (full 55-80 sources, premier 100-130) baked into the prompt text. Step 1 extracts atomic items, literal required H2 headings, period-pinned filings, tier, response format, citation style and posture levers, then checks every query phrase against a coverage matrix. In step 2 the lead itself plans and runs 40-100 searches across breadth, canonical, adversarial and period-filing lenses. It then sends URL batches to 10-12 Sonnet fetchers, which read full pages, write summaries and claims with verbatim quotes, and chase 3-8 cited primaries each. Gap waves, a redundancy audit and ranking commands follow. Step 3 pairs contradicting claims inline, and step 4 runs 2-3 loci analysts and allocates depth budgets. Code enforces almost none of steps 1-4: the ship gate checks only step 1's headings and length band.

mechanisms.name: Bootstrap installer skill
mechanisms.what: Checks the hyperresearch CLI and picks the Claude Code or Codex branch. Runs `hyperresearch install`, which writes skills, agents, a CLAUDE.md block and a PreToolUse hook into the project, then hands off to the router with the request verbatim.
mechanisms.why: Setup only; it does not change how research is done.
mechanisms.cost: One-time pip install (Python 3.11-3.14). Edits the user's CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.json, and the new skill may need a session restart before it is visible (:66-73).

mechanisms.name: Per-step skill loading (router as sequencer)
mechanisms.what: The router calls Skill(hyperresearch-N-...) for each step (on Codex it reads the step file with cat), so each procedure is loaded fresh just before use. The router itself holds only sequencing, rules and recovery.
mechanisms.why: It stops steps being silently dropped after compaction, which was their V7 failure. The only evidence offered compares two different benchmark questions (Q57 55.9 vs Q9 52.6), so the size of the effect is unproven.
mechanisms.cost: 18 step files of 4-23 KB, about 1-6k tokens each, are loaded over a run. Keeping 18 files consistent is real upkeep, and they already drift (stale step pointers, enum mismatches).

mechanisms.name: Install-time profile rendering (gears)
mechanisms.what: Prompts are Jinja templates with << >> delimiters and StrictUndefined. At install, the persisted gear becomes `p`, every other profile is reachable by name, and `platform` branches the text. `profile use` re-renders the prompts for the next run.
mechanisms.why: One template serves both full (55-80 sources) and premier (100-130, double depth), and a typo fails the tests. But the numbers are fixed per install, and a light-tier run reads the gear's numbers.
mechanisms.cost: No runtime cost. Moderate complexity: four profiles, config overlays and golden fixtures. Changing gear means re-rendering.

mechanisms.name: Tier classification and routing
mechanisms.what: Step 1 labels the query light or full from signal words (default full; tier up when unsure); dissertation runs only on request. The router runs light as steps 1, 2, 10, 15, 16 and full as everything. The ship gate takes its required steps from the decomposition's tier.
mechanisms.why: It sizes the effort to the query: light skips the contradiction graph, loci, depth work, critics and cite-check. That trade-off rests on one model judgement, and there is no middle tier since `standard` was removed (CHANGELOG.md:364).
mechanisms.cost: Light takes about 30-40 min, full about 1.5-2.5 h (profiles.py:306, 324): a difference of about 11 steps and dozens of subagents.

mechanisms.name: Run manifest, todo list and resume
mechanisms.what: `run init` writes run.json, and the orchestrator records each step with `run step`. `run resume` returns the next step for the declared tier, with a per-step artifact table as fallback. TodoWrite holds 16 numbered items.
mechanisms.why: It keeps a 2-hour run on track after compaction or a crash, as long as the agent records its steps honestly.
mechanisms.cost: About two CLI calls per step; negligible tokens.

mechanisms.name: Canonical query file and spawn contract
mechanisms.what: The query is saved verbatim to query.md. Every subagent prompt carries the block-quoted query, one sentence on its pipeline position, its inputs, and its role shim pasted verbatim.
mechanisms.why: It prevents paraphrase drift across 15-45 subagents and makes each spawn self-contained.
mechanisms.cost: The query plus shim, a few hundred to about 1.5k tokens, is repeated in every spawn.

mechanisms.name: Posture levers and role shims
mechanisms.what: Step 1 picks a register (teach/survey/analyze/advocate), writes 2-3 sentences of domain notes, and sets an inference depth (surface/standard/deep). levers.py builds research, drafting, critics and polish shims from fixed text blocks. Step 4 may raise the depth and re-render them.
mechanisms.why: Every downstream agent gets the same voice and evidence norms. For example, 'deep' allows gray literature with provenance, and 'survey' stops critics demanding a thesis. Fixed text also avoids the lead paraphrasing the posture.
mechanisms.cost: Tiny: one CLI call and about 150-400 tokens per spawn.

mechanisms.name: Atomic decomposition with literal required headings
mechanisms.what: Extracts sub-questions, entities with required fields, formats, sections, time horizons, period-pinned periods and scope. Produces an ordered, never-empty list of literal H2 headings that mirror the prompt's enumerated asks. The ship gate checks each heading appears verbatim in the report.
mechanisms.why: Instruction-following judges reward a report whose structure matches the prompt. The author calls this the single highest-leverage input, and the gate makes it binding.
mechanisms.cost: A small inline pass (about 5-15k output tokens, my estimate).

mechanisms.name: Coverage matrix self-audit and search gap check
mechanisms.what: Maps every significant query phrase to an atomic item with a scope check: no narrowing, and both readings of an ambiguous phrase. Loops until there are zero gaps. Step 2 then checks that every matrix row has at least one planned search.
mechanisms.why: Catches early and cheaply the common failure where a query term never gets a search and therefore never gets a section.
mechanisms.cost: One inline table and a re-check. It is prompt-only; no code verifies it.

mechanisms.name: Period-pinned primary filings (Lens D)
mechanisms.what: Step 1 extracts each named reporting period with its expected primary filing. Step 2 must plan a search for that exact filing (EDGAR, Companies House or a dated release, not a transcript). Fetchers fetch the document for that exact period and copy table figures verbatim, without rounding.
mechanisms.why: For financial and regulatory questions the exact figures exist only in the filing for that period, and transcripts round them.
mechanisms.cost: A few extra searches and fetches per named period.

mechanisms.name: Multi-lens search plan with adversarial floor
mechanisms.what: For each atomic item the lead plans breadth, canonical/academic, adversarial and, where periods apply, filing searches in a lensed table: 40-100 at full gear, 80-160 at premier. At least 5 (premier 8) must be adversarial, and the lead must run all of them itself.
mechanisms.why: Spreads sources across every item, and brings in critics and primary literature that topic-only searching misses.
mechanisms.cost: 40-160 WebSearch calls inside the lead's own context, roughly 1-2k tokens each by my estimate, plus a PreToolUse reminder on every call.

mechanisms.name: Pre-fetch utility scoring
mechanisms.what: The lead scores 80-120 candidate URLs on six 0-3 dimensions from search snippets. Fetchers pass the score to `fetch --utility-score`, and it becomes 20% of the note's quality_score.
mechanisms.why: At full gear the batches hold 80-144 URLs, at least the size of the 60-100 deduplicated queue, so selection removes almost nothing. The scores are guesses from snippets.
mechanisms.cost: A moderate inline table of about 100 rows by 6 columns, several thousand tokens.

mechanisms.name: URL-batch fetcher waves
mechanisms.what: The deduplicated URLs are split into non-overlapping batches. Wave 1 spawns 10-12 Sonnet fetchers in one message (premier 14-18). The coverage check then spawns 3-5 gap fetchers, and the redundancy audit may add 2-3 more.
mechanisms.why: Builds, in parallel, the corpus that every later step depends on.
mechanisms.cost: The biggest cost of the front half: about 15-20 Sonnet agents, and an estimated 700-1,500 tool calls in wave 1 alone.

mechanisms.name: Fetcher per-source processing and claims extraction
mechanisms.what: For each URL a fetcher checks for duplicates, fetches it with the CLI and reads the full body. It deprecates junk and off-topic pages, then writes tags, a summary sized to the source's density, and a claims JSON of 3-25 claims. Each claim carries a stance, numbers, entities and a verbatim quoted_support.
mechanisms.why: Summaries let the lead see the corpus without reading bodies. The verbatim quotes feed the evidence digest and the quote-integrity gate.
mechanisms.cost: Each fetcher reads 15-20 full bodies (about 100-300k tokens of source text, my estimate) and writes 10-60k tokens.

mechanisms.name: Mandatory primary-source chasing with provenance breadcrumbs
mechanisms.what: After its batch, each fetcher picks the 3-8 most promising cited primaries by authority, specificity and how often they are cited. It finds them (with WebSearch when only author and title are known), fetches them with --suggested-by and processes them the same way, up to 8.
mechanisms.why: Replaces secondary commentary with the studies and data it cites, which raises source authority.
mechanisms.cost: Adds 30-96 fetches in wave 1 at full gear and overshoots the 55-80 target. It also conflicts with the spawn prompt's 'do not search'.

mechanisms.name: Fetch layer: open-access rescue, junk detection, escalation queue
mechanisms.what: `hpr fetch` detects login and bot walls and first tries a legal open-access copy (Unpaywall, Europe PMC, CORE). A thin page with a DOI is swapped for the full text, with the swap disclosed. URLs that stay blocked go to a browser-lane queue instead of being lost.
mechanisms.why: Paywalled papers get read in full instead of cited from their abstracts, and the remaining failures show up as visible gaps.
mechanisms.cost: Extra HTTP lookups for each blocked or thin page; no LLM cost.

mechanisms.name: Browser-lane escalation (Claude Code only)
mechanisms.what: One browser-fetcher at a time drives the user's Chrome through Claude-in-Chrome to drain up to 10 queued blocked URLs. It never attempts CAPTCHAs, logins or 2FA; it collects those into a single message for the user.
mechanisms.why: Reaches login-gated and bot-walled sources, which matters most for niche and paywalled topics.
mechanisms.cost: Serial and human-paced, and it can interrupt the user. Not available on Codex.

mechanisms.name: Long-source delegation to source-analyst
mechanisms.what: A relevant source of more than about 5,000 words gets its own Sonnet agent. It reads the whole body and writes a structured note: thesis, method, findings with numbers, citations, caveats and quotes. Up to 6 such agents (premier 10).
mechanisms.why: Long papers and reports get a careful, dense digest instead of a skimmed summary.
mechanisms.cost: Up to 6-10 large-context spawns. The prompt itself calls a 60k-word read one of the most expensive spawns.

mechanisms.name: Coverage check and redundancy audit
mechanisms.what: After wave 1 the lead counts sources per item (4+, 2-3, 1, 0) and fills thin items. At full tier it also reads every claims file and clusters derivative sources (more than 60% shared quotes, or shared suggested-by ancestry). Derivatives are discounted, and items left with fewer than 2 independent sources get another wave.
mechanisms.why: Targets gaps and catches one source copied many times. But the thresholds are soft ('thin is acceptable'), and the audit loads every claim into the lead's context.
mechanisms.cost: The coverage map is cheap. The redundancy audit reads every claims file, an estimated 100k+ tokens on a full corpus.

mechanisms.name: Ranking signals (claims DB, DOI, citations, retractions, PageRank)
mechanisms.what: Four CLI commands: ingest claims into SQLite with full-text search, backfill DOIs, fetch citation counts and retraction flags, and compute vault PageRank plus a composite quality_score. The weights are tier 35%, utility 20%, authority 25% and centrality 20%; retracted sources are floored.
mechanisms.why: The retraction floor and citation authority are useful. Centrality, however, is inverted for breadcrumb links, so it rewards hubs over the primaries the pipeline chased.
mechanisms.cost: Seconds locally plus cached API calls; no LLM cost.

mechanisms.name: Contradiction graph and consensus claims
mechanisms.what: The lead loads every claims file and pairs claims that oppose each other: same stance target with opposite stance, same entities with opposite conclusions, or different numbers for the same scope. It clusters the pairs into ranked fights and writes consensus claims weighted by independence scores.
mechanisms.why: Grounds dialectical loci in actual disagreement rather than intuition. But the pairing is LLM work over hundreds of claims, and the independence math overweights syndicated clusters.
mechanisms.cost: A large inline context (all the claims again) plus one CLI call.

mechanisms.name: Parallel loci analysis with dynamic depth budgets
mechanisms.what: 2-3 Sonnet analysts each propose 1-8 loci (convergent or dialectical) from summaries, the contradiction graph and the claims. The lead dedupes and clamps them to 6 (premier 10). It scores importance, uncertainty, disagreement and decision impact, splits 40 (80) depth sources by brackets, sets the investigator count, and may raise the inference depth.
mechanisms.why: Points the expensive depth step at questions that are both contested and decision-relevant, and the dialectical requirement forces the report to engage with disagreement.
mechanisms.cost: 2-3 Sonnet agents, whose cost depends on how much of each note they read, plus an inline scoring pass.

mechanisms.name: Ship gate as the only path to done
mechanisms.why: Hard blocks on fabricated quotes and retracted citations protect accuracy. For steps 1-4 it checks only step 1's headings, length band and shim files.
mechanisms.cost: One CLI call plus any fix rounds.

mechanisms.name: Completion guards (Codex Stop hook; Claude 'never bare text' rule)
mechanisms.what: On Codex, a Stop hook blocks the session from ending, once per attempt, while the newest run still has a next step. On Claude Code there is only an instruction to include a tool call in every response while subagents run.
mechanisms.why: Stops Codex from answering inline and quitting. On Claude Code, finishing the run rests on the model alone.
mechanisms.cost: Negligible.

mechanisms.name: PreToolUse vault reminder hook
mechanisms.what: A Node script adds a reminder on every WebSearch and WebFetch call: check the vault first, and use `hpr fetch` instead of WebFetch.
mechanisms.why: Advisory only. It may steer the agent toward vault search and the fetch CLI.
mechanisms.cost: About 100 tokens per web tool call, and it needs Node on PATH.

mechanisms.name: Chapter partition (dissertation)
mechanisms.what: Groups atomic items into 4-10 chapters of 40-80 sources each and registers them in the manifest. Steps 2-10 then loop per chapter, two at a time, before a global reconcile and synthesis.
mechanisms.why: Experimental. Its length and citation targets are not wired, and the length gate measures it against the argumentative band.
mechanisms.cost: Multiplies steps 2-10 by the chapter count. The roadmap estimates $200-500 per run (docs/roadmap-2.0/phase-3-dissertation-scale.md:133).

ideas_for_vafer: Adopt a phrase-level scope check in plan.md: map each significant query phrase to a checklist row, and count any narrowing as a gap (from decompose.md:162-179).
Adopt period-pinned rows: when the question names a fiscal period or a dated event, add a row for the filing of that exact period and point one scout query at it.

Keep VAFER's thin lead: researchers do the searching and reading, and the lead sees only summaries of at most 300 words. This is VAFER's main structural edge over hyperresearch, whose lead runs every search and loads every claim.
Keep researchers owning sub-questions, not URL batches, so each researcher answers for the coverage of its own row.
Replace a global adversarial count with one criticism or counter-evidence query per contested row.
Adapt citation chasing in briefs: ask each researcher to follow up to N primary sources cited by secondary pages and note 'found via <URL>'.
Add a one-line posture field to plan.md (teach, survey, analyze or advocate) to set the report's voice; skip the four-file shim machinery.
Add a light 'loci' pass: after wave 1, rank OPEN, PARTIAL and CONFLICT rows by decision impact times uncertainty, and spend the gap wave on the top 1-3.
For contested topics, require at least one CONFLICT row to be examined with each side's best evidence (taken from the dialectical-locus invariant).
Adopt a legal open-access fallback for paywalled papers (Unpaywall, Europe PMC, CORE), and disclose any substitution in the notes.
Do not add numeric targets the agent cannot check; keep only rules checkable in one pass (every [n] resolves, every quoted string appears in notes).
Skip pre-fetch utility scoring: it costs tokens and prunes almost nothing in hyperresearch.
Skip PageRank and composite quality scores (hyperresearch's centrality is inverted); label each source primary or secondary instead.
Keep 'copies of one account count once', and do not copy hyperresearch's 1/k-per-member weighting, which makes five reprints count as 1.8.
Keep three tiers: hyperresearch's light/full cliff (5 vs 16 steps, about 30 min vs about 2 h) is exactly the gap VAFER's Standard tier fills.
Put each tier's numbers only in that tier's own section, so a lighter tier never reads a heavier tier's counts.
Key reuse by topic and question through INDEX.md, not by a per-run tag; hyperresearch's tag scoping hides prior-run sources from new runs.
Never offer an output option the final check rejects (hyperresearch's citation_style 'none').
Keep instructions shell-agnostic with no Node dependency: hyperresearch's bash snippets and Node hook break on Windows and on Codex under PowerShell.
Do not rely on one turn lasting hours; keep a Deep run resumable from plan.md with a single 'next action' line.
Do not split SKILL.md into per-step files while it stays short (83 lines); hyperresearch did that only after one prompt grew to 1,200 lines and lost steps to compaction.

key_claims.claim: In steps 1-4, code enforces only the step-1 outputs that the ship gate reads: literal required headings, the response-format length band and the shim files. Source minimums, per-item coverage, the adversarial floor, the zero-gap coverage matrix and the dialectical-locus invariant are prompt text, with explicit 'proceed anyway' escape hatches.

The lead runs the 40-100 planned searches, scores 80-120 URLs, and reads every claims file in its own context twice (steps 2.6 and 3). Fetchers are told not to search, and each must report every summary back to the lead.

Scale numbers are written into the skill text at install time from a single gear (`p`). A light-tier run therefore sees full-gear counts in the step-2 procedure, and light's planned_searches, candidate_urls and deduped_urls are never rendered anywhere.

The independence audit weights a cluster of k copies at 1 + (k-1)/k, so five reprints count as 1.8 voices. This contradicts step 3's 'count each cluster as ONE voice' and the README's 'weight of one source'.

Vault PageRank credits the secondary or hub note that suggested a source, not the primary that was chased, because the --suggested-by breadcrumb link is written into the chased note's body. Centrality is 20% of quality_score and is computed only once, at step 2.7.

Fetchers skip any URL already in the vault from an earlier run without adding the current run's tag, and every run-scoped step selects notes by that exact tag. Prior-run sources therefore never count toward coverage, loci or curation.

pipeline-back.subsystem: hyperresearch back half: critics (step 12), gap fetch (13), tool-locked patcher (14), cite-check (14.5), polish (15), readability audit (16), the final ship gate, and the subagent roster
pipeline-back.summary: Steps 12-16 are hyperresearch's correction layer after synthesis. Four Opus critics (dialectic, depth, width, instruction) read the synthesized report and the vault and write capped findings JSON (12/12/10/15 at the full gear) without exact patches. The instruction critic also checks H2 order against the decomposition. A conditional gap fetch (at most 5 gaps, 2-4 Sonnet fetchers) runs when a finding's topic has 0-1 vault notes. One Opus patcher applies findings as Edits into a pre-stubbed log and sends H2 restructures to the orchestrator; it is tool-locked to Read+Edit on Claude Code, prose-only on Codex. Cite-check (14.5) pairs citations with sentences in Python and auto-passes pairs whose numbers or 6-word shingles appear in the cited note's claims. It marks dangling citations critical, has a Sonnet checker judge the rest, then runs a second patcher pass. An Opus polish auditor strips pipeline leaks, meta-discourse, filler and hedges. An Opus recommender proposes up to 50 readability edits that the orchestrator applies selectively. The binding gate (run finish) checks length, headings, citation density, quote integrity, retractions and file existence. Fixing critical findings is honor-system. mechanisms.name: Four parallel adversarial critics (findings-only JSON)
mechanisms.what: Dialectic, depth, width and instruction critics are spawned in one parallel message against the synthesized report. Each writes {critic_type, findings:[severity, location, issue, evidence, recommendation]} with no old_text/new_text patches. Caps: 12/12/10/15 (full), 16/16/14/18 (premier), 24/24/20/30 (dissertation). The step may proceed with a partial set, but the instruction critic must not be skipped.
mechanisms.why: The only substance review after synthesis. Finding and fixing are separated and each critic has a distinct angle. Nothing in the repo measures their effect, and findings matter only if the patcher applies them.
mechanisms.cost: 4 Opus subagents. Each reads the full 5-16K-word report plus vault searches; search --json returns up to 20 full note bodies per query (src/hyperresearch/cli/search.py:176-186, core/config.py:229). Estimated tens to hundreds of thousands of input tokens per critic, not measured.

mechanisms.name: Instruction critic: noun-phrase coverage, decomposition-gap and structural-mirror check
mechanisms.what: Extracts every noun phrase, imperative and format cue from the verbatim query. Flags decomposition narrowing as a critical 'decomposition-gap'. Compares ordered '## ' headings element-wise with required_section_headings; each mismatch is critical with requires_orchestrator_restructure: true. Then checks per-item coverage, format, order and sufficiency, 'vague-recommendation', and readability-structural checks R1-R6 (definitions, body citation density, forward analysis, comparison tables, section primers, comparison axes; max 3).
mechanisms.why: Targets prompt adherence, which the authors call the widest-variance dimension (skills/hyperresearch-12-critics.md:60). It is anchored to the verbatim query, and its structural fixes go to an agent with Write access (skills/hyperresearch-14-patcher.md:129-138).
mechanisms.cost: One Opus agent with a 16.2K-char prompt. It mostly reads the query, decomposition and draft, so it is cheaper than the vault-searching critics.

mechanisms.name: Depth critic: interim-note usage and compressed-mechanism check
mechanisms.what: Lists every depth-investigator interim note and checks that each Synthesis's numbers, quotes, mechanisms and disagreements reached the draft. A developed quantitative mechanism compressed to a bare mention is a major finding. The evidence field must cite the interim note.
mechanisms.why: Recovers evidence the depth budget already paid for, which is a plausible insight gain. The effect is not measured.
mechanisms.cost: One Opus agent reading every interim note (up to 6 at full, 10 at premier) plus the draft.

mechanisms.name: Dialectic critic with register-conditional standards
mechanisms.what: Searches the vault for notes that contradict or complicate the draft's positions. Critical means the draft contradicts the vault's own evidence. In teach/survey register it flags unfair representation instead of missing commitment; in advocate register a weak steel-man is critical.
mechanisms.why: Bringing counter-evidence in raises argumentative quality, and register awareness stops critics from undoing the chosen mode. The authors claim +2.5 RACE from register alone on one query (CHANGELOG.md:194).
mechanisms.cost: One Opus agent making repeated search -j calls that return full bodies.

mechanisms.name: Width critic with bloat detection
mechanisms.what: Clusters the vault by tag and title. Cross-checks the query's noun phrases, temp/coverage-gaps.md and the decomposition against the draft's sections, and skims 2-3 notes per gap cluster. Also emits up to 2 bloat findings (dilution, exec-summary/conclusion repetition), justified by benchmark report-size averages.
mechanisms.why: Catches parts of the topic the draft dropped. The bloat check pushes back against the other critics' additions, but only with 2 findings.
mechanisms.cost: One Opus agent; note list --all -j over 55-130 notes plus skims.

mechanisms.name: Post-critic gap fetch (step 13)
mechanisms.what: The orchestrator scans findings by failure_mode and severity, keyword-searches the vault, and treats 0-1 relevant notes as fetch-worthy. It caps at 5 gaps (8 premier, 10 dissertation), writes 2-3 web queries per gap, and spawns 2-4 fetchers tagged post-critic-fill. New claims go into the evidence digest under '### Post-critic gap fill'; results are logged to temp/post-critic-fetch-log.md.
mechanisms.why: Gives the patcher evidence to cite instead of fabricating. But the trigger is ill-defined, the unfilled-gap flags never reach the patcher, and the authors expect it to be a near-no-op.
mechanisms.cost: Vault searches in the orchestrator's own context (up to 20 full bodies each with --json), plus 0-4 Sonnet fetchers. Each fetcher must chase up to 8 primary sources (core/hooks.py:3152-3158, 3198).

mechanisms.name: Tool-locked patcher (Read+Edit) with surgical-edit and integrate-don't-caveat rules
mechanisms.what: One Opus patcher merges all findings and sorts them by severity, sends restructure findings to escalation, spot-checks evidence ids, and dedupes. It applies minimal Edits with a verbatim old_string, matches the citation style, and prefers scoping a claim ('X holds in A; in B, Y because Z') over appending caveats. It logs to a pre-stubbed patch-log.json. The orchestrator treats a skipped critical as a pipeline blocker.
mechanisms.why: On Claude Code the lock stops wholesale rewrites that would lose the synthesized draft, and integrate-by-scoping is a sound writing rule. Edit size is not capped (hooks.py:1408-1411).
mechanisms.cost: One Opus agent reading up to 49 findings (full), the report and the evidence digest, with at least one Edit turn per applied finding.

mechanisms.name: Pre-stubbed JSON logs (patch-log, polish-log, cite-check-patch-log)
mechanisms.what: The orchestrator writes canonical empty JSON stubs with echo so the Edit-only agents can fill them. If a stub stays empty, it parses the JSON out of the Task result and writes the log via Bash.
mechanisms.why: Bookkeeping forced by the Edit-only lock. The stubs also satisfy the gate's existence-only checks.
mechanisms.cost: Small, but adds complexity and bash snippets that break on Windows.

mechanisms.name: Orchestrator structural restructure (14.4) and polish escalations (15.3)
mechanisms.what: The orchestrator, which holds Write and Edit, moves, renames or inserts H2s for orchestrator_escalated findings and polish escalations. It keeps section bodies, writes short evidence-grounded paragraphs for new headings, and logs changes in orchestrator-restructure-log.md.
mechanisms.why: Fixes heading and format mismatches the judge rewards, which the Edit-only agents cannot do safely.
mechanisms.cost: Edit calls in the main context. The 15.3 fixes land after cite-check and are never re-verified.

mechanisms.name: Cite-check mechanical triage (citecheck extract)
mechanisms.what: Python splits sentences and binds markers to notes: [N] through the Sources list by exact URL or exact title, [[id]] through note ids. Unresolved entries are marked dangling (critical). A pair auto-passes when all its 2+-character numbers, or one 6-word shingle, appear in the cited note's claims. All 'strong' pairs plus 60% of weak pairs are sampled for the LLM.
mechanisms.why: Cheap dangling-citation detection is valuable. But auto-pass leaks: citation-marker digits count as numbers, matching runs against the whole note's claims blob, and unmapped [N] markers are silently dropped.
mechanisms.cost: Negligible compute (one CLI call). Its false auto-passes cost accuracy, not tokens.

mechanisms.name: Skeptical cite-checker and second patcher pass
mechanisms.what: A Sonnet checker reads each cited note via 'note show' and judges supported, partially-supported, unsupported or wrong-source, defaulting skeptical and judging only the source-sentence binding. Unsupported number-bearing claims and wrong-source are critical. A second Opus patcher pass swaps citations, softens claims or deletes sentences. The checker gets no register shim.
mechanisms.why: The pipeline's only claim-level faithfulness check, aimed at what FACT-style evaluators measure. Its value is limited by the triage bugs, by running before polish, and by an existence-only gate.
mechanisms.cost: 1-2 Sonnet agents (the second only above about 40 pairs), reading full note bodies 5 ids per call. Every [N] pair counts as strong, so all non-auto-passed pairs go to the LLM. Plus one more Opus patcher spawn.

mechanisms.name: Polish auditor (hygiene, pipeline-vocabulary denylist, meta-discourse, filler, hedge-striking)
mechanisms.what: An Opus Read+Edit agent that strips scaffold sections, YAML, prompt echoes and non-verbatim quotation marks, and rewrites a denylist of pipeline terms (Locus N, Tension N, comparisons.md, ...). It deletes meta-discourse and filler, strikes hedges where cited evidence sits in the same paragraph, removes exec-summary/synthesis repetition, and splits long sentences and paragraphs. It must not touch Sources.

The orchestrator applies them by apply/judgment/skeptical/skip heuristics, in a fixed order, by direct Edit, and logs readability-decisions.json.

mechanisms.name: Binding ship gate: run finish / verify_run

Up to 3 fix rounds, otherwise the run is blocked.
mechanisms.why: Quote-integrity is a real mechanical block on hallucinated quotes. Most other checks are weak, check existence only, or can be satisfied by stub files.

mechanisms.name: Register and inference shims pasted into critics, patcher, polish and recommender

ideas_for_vafer: Adopt a prompt-adherence critic that diffs the report against the verbatim question's named entities, sub-questions and format cues; check heading order with a script and use the model only for semantic coverage.
Adopt findings-only reviewers that output location/issue/evidence/recommendation, capped at about 10-15 findings each, so the load-bearing findings are not buried.
Adopt the depth critic's check for a developed quantitative mechanism compressed to a bare mention; it is cheap and targets insight directly.
Adopt 'integrate by scoping, don't append caveats' as a writing rule for VAFER's 'Where sources disagree' section.
Keep VAFER's verify-last rule; never run hedge-stripping or readability edits after verification, and if an edit is unavoidable, re-verify only the sentences it touched.
Avoid removing hedges just because a citation is present; set claim strength from the source wording the check confirmed.
Adapt cite-check pairing, fixed: strip markers before extracting numbers, match numbers within the same claim or quote rather than the whole note, and normalize URLs.
Make an unresolvable [n] marker a hard error, never a silent drop; every [n] must map to a sources entry with an opened URL, and every entry must be cited.
Count citation density on the body only, never including the sources list.
Adopt a mechanical quote check against the saved note of the cited source, not any note; VAFER notes already keep verbatim quotes of 30 words or less, so a script can grep them.
Avoid gates that check whether files exist; require a record for every critical finding id (applied, rejected with a reason, or escalated) and let the script verify it.
Do not make correctness depend on per-agent tool allowlists; they hold on one host only, and hyperresearch locks the wrong agents. Check diff size and the verified-sentence set after edits instead.
Avoid search calls that dump full bodies into the orchestrator; keep notes as summaries plus quotes and load bodies on demand inside researchers.
When a gap wave fails, carry 'not found after these queries' into the writer's inputs; hyperresearch logs it to a file its patcher never reads.
Fix length before verification, never with a full regeneration after it.
Adapt register levers (teach/survey/analyze/advocate) to decide whether reviewers demand commitment; cheap, and the authors claim it matters a lot to RACE judges.
Adapt the readability pass as a script lint (paragraph and sentence length, a table for comparisons of 3+ entities on 2+ dimensions, no horizontal rules) that runs before verification, not after it.
Never expose internal pipeline vocabulary to the writer, rather than paying a polish pass to scrub it; grep a short denylist before delivery.
Validate the sources list too: no truncated titles, URL present, access date present; hyperresearch ships truncated titles because Sources are off-limits to polish.
Avoid bash-only snippets in skill prose (echo > stubs, VAR=x cmd prefixes, python -c without encoding=); write shell-neutral steps or give both syntaxes for Windows.
Make the citation check a numbered, required step in VAFER's flow and done criteria, not a half-step that resume logic can skip.

key_claims.claim: The cite-check mechanical triage auto-passes sentences on number substrings. The citation marker's own digits count as the sentence's numbers and are matched against the cited note's whole claims blob, so a non-numeric sentence citing [23] passes when '23' appears anywhere in that note's claims (e.g. '2023'). Every [N]-cited sentence is also flagged 'strong', so the 0.6 sample rate never applies to inline style.

key_claims.claim: run finish never checks that critical findings were applied. cite-check-resolved passes when cite-check-patch-log.json exists, and the orchestrator pre-stubs that file before the patcher runs. Critic and patch artifacts are checked for existence only. The patch-surgery lint is not part of the gate.

Edits that change claim strength happen after cite-check and are never re-verified: polish hedge-stripping ('X tends to cause Y [3][5]' becomes 'X causes Y [3][5]'), step 16 merges and splits, and the length-fix synthesizer rewrite at the gate.
Step 14.5 is not in any profile's step list. run resume therefore goes from 14 to 15, the Codex Stop hook ignores 14.5, and verify_run checks cite-check only if 14.5 was recorded as done.

The tool lock (Read+Edit) is real only on Claude Code and only for the patcher and polish auditor. It blocks Write and Bash but not edit size: no per-hunk cap exists, despite README. The critics and the readability recommender hold Write while being told they cannot change the report. On Codex every lock is prose.

Gap fetch selects findings by a failure_mode field that only the instruction critic emits. It logs unfilled gaps to a file the patcher never receives, and its vault check uses search --json, which returns up to 20 full note bodies into the orchestrator's context.

verification.subsystem: Cite-check, claims, independence audit, similarity, untrusted content, source ranking
verification.summary: hyperresearch's fact layer. Sonnet fetchers write per-source claim JSON (claims, 'verbatim' quoted_support, numbers, stance); Python ingests it into SQLite with full-text search, once, at step 2. At step 14.5 (full and dissertation tiers) Python splits the final report into (sentence, cited note) pairs and auto-passes a pair when its numbers, or any 6-word window, appear as substrings in the cited note's extracted claims. Citations resolving to no note are flagged dangling, and the rest go to a Sonnet cite-checker. It reads each cited note's full body and returns supported, partially-supported, unsupported or wrong-source; an Opus patcher applies swap, soften or delete edits. The ship gate hard-blocks fabricated quotes and unacknowledged retracted wikilink citations, but for cite-check only checks that files exist. An independence audit clusters syndicated copies (canonical URL, wire-service opening, near-duplicate bodies) and scores members 1/k, for a consensus rule the LLM applies. Fetched bodies are fenced in <untrusted-source> tags on two read paths. PageRank plus a tier, utility, authority and centrality composite reorders search results for reading lists. Only the LLM checker reads sources against sentences; the mechanical parts are weaker than documented.

mechanisms.name: Claim extraction by fetchers
mechanisms.what: Each Sonnet fetcher writes claims-<note-id>.json per source: 3-25 one-sentence claims with stance, stance_target, evidence_type, scope, a 'verbatim' quoted_support, numbers and confidence.
mechanisms.why: Feeds the evidence digest, the step-3 contradiction graph and the cite-check triage blob. Quotes are never verified against the page, so extraction errors travel downstream as trusted evidence.
mechanisms.cost: Output tokens inside each fetcher run (3-25 claims per source); one Write per source.

mechanisms.name: Claims ingest and store
mechanisms.what: Python ingests claims JSON into a claims table plus claims_fts, idempotent on (note_id, sha256(claim)[:16]). Hardened against hostile JSON: 8 MB file cap, 20k chars per field, type coercion, path containment. Drops scope, entities, time and region fields, never checks quoted_support against the body, and runs only once, at step 2.
mechanisms.why: The substrate for mechanical triage and wrong-source search. Its gaps (no re-ingest after step 13, single-object files dropped silently) shrink what both can see.
mechanisms.cost: Milliseconds; one CLI call per run.

mechanisms.name: Claims full-text search
mechanisms.what: `claims search` passes the raw query to FTS5 MATCH with no quoting or error handling. The cite-checker uses it to find the correct note for wrong-source findings.
mechanisms.why: Enables swap-citation fixes, but phrases containing hyphens, %, periods, apostrophes or colons raise sqlite3.OperationalError (probe), so this path is unreliable.
mechanisms.cost: One tool call per lookup, plus retries after crashes.

mechanisms.name: Sentence-citation pair extraction
mechanisms.what: Regex-splits the report body (everything before ## Sources or ## References) into sentences. Binds each [N] to a note through the Sources list (exact URL, then exact title) and each [[note-id]] by exact id. Unresolved Sources entries become dangling. Numbers are taken from the raw sentence, citation markers included.
mechanisms.why: Defines what can be checked at all. It silently drops an [N] with no Sources entry, drops every numbered citation when the Sources format is non-standard, and merges sentences in Turkish, CJK or citation-after-period text.
mechanisms.cost: Milliseconds of Python; one CLI call (`citecheck extract`).

mechanisms.name: Mechanical triage (auto-pass)
mechanisms.what: Auto-passes a pair when every number of 2+ characters in the sentence is a substring of the cited note's claims blob, or, if there are no such numbers, when any 6-word window appears in it. Otherwise the pair goes to the LLM. A pair with no resolved note is dangling.
mechanisms.why: Saves LLM reads but passes wrong numbers ('5%' inside '25%', citation index '12' inside '2012'; probe), judged against unverified LLM-extracted claims. Auto-passed pairs never reach the checker (hooks.py:3552).
mechanisms.cost: Negligible CPU; saves an unknown share of LLM reads.

mechanisms.name: Deterministic sampling of the LLM tier
mechanisms.what: Keeps 100% of 'strong' pairs and a floor-stepped 60% of the rest, with no RNG, so results are reproducible across resumes.
mechanisms.why: A pair is 'strong' if its sentence contains any digit, including the [N] marker itself, so on the example report 155 of 155 pairs are strong and nothing is sampled away. The design's profile-configurable rate (phase-5-verification.md:29) is not implemented.
mechanisms.cost: None, and in practice no LLM savings for reports with numbered citations.

mechanisms.name: LLM cite-checker (step 14.5)
mechanisms.what: A Sonnet subagent (two in parallel above about 40 pairs) reads each cited note's full body via `note show -j`, up to 5 ids per call. It returns supported, partially-supported, unsupported or wrong-source, judging the binding rather than truth, with a skeptical default. Critical means unsupported number-bearing or wrong-source; everything else is major.
mechanisms.why: The only component that reads source text against report sentences, so the only one that can catch unsupported or mis-attributed citations.
mechanisms.cost: 1-2 Sonnet runs. Estimate: 0.3-0.8M input tokens of body text for a report citing about 97 notes (the example report), more with duplicate reads across the split and re-reads of long bodies. Roughly 20-40 Bash calls plus claims-search calls.

mechanisms.name: Second patcher pass
mechanisms.what: The orchestrator appends dangling citations as critical findings, pre-creates cite-check-patch-log.json, and spawns the Opus patcher (Read and Edit only) to swap the citation, soften the claim or delete the sentence.
mechanisms.why: Turns findings into text changes; without it the checker's verdicts change nothing. Whether critical findings get applied is enforced only by instruction.
mechanisms.cost: One Opus subagent reading the report (about 15k tokens for an 11k-word report) and the findings, plus several Edit calls.

mechanisms.name: Ship gate: cite-check-resolved
mechanisms.what: In `run finish`, if the manifest marks step 14.5 done, cite-check-findings.json must exist and parse; if any finding is critical, cite-check-patch-log.json must exist.
mechanisms.why: Never reads the log's contents, so the orchestrator's pre-created stub satisfies it. Skipping step 14.5 also skips the check.
mechanisms.cost: Negligible.

mechanisms.name: quote-integrity hard block
mechanisms.what: Every double-quoted span of 5+ words in the report body must match a porter-stemmed FTS5 phrase in some note's body_plain. Any error blocks `run finish`.
mechanisms.why: Stops fabricated or mangled quotes from shipping. Weakened because a match in any note counts, including LLM-written interim notes (sync.py:309-313), and because the remedy lets the orchestrator just strip the quotation marks (skills/hyperresearch.md:277).
mechanisms.cost: One FTS query per quote; milliseconds.

mechanisms.name: retracted-citations hard block and retraction sweep
mechanisms.what: Blocks a cited retracted source unless the word 'retract' appears within 200 characters. Scans only [[wikilink]] citations. Retraction flags come from a fresh OpenAlex / Semantic Scholar sweep of notes that have a DOI.
mechanisms.why: Catches a rare but serious failure in wikilink reports. Reports with [N] citations and sources without a DOI are never checked.
mechanisms.cost: API calls at ship time (rate-limited without S2_API_KEY); one CLI call.

mechanisms.name: numeric-consistency lint (advisory)
mechanisms.what: Flags report numbers (decimals, numbers of 4+ digits, percentages) that appear as a substring nowhere in all claims plus all sourced note bodies. Warning only.
mechanisms.why: Substring matching across the whole vault makes recall near zero in a large vault, and the lint never blocks.
mechanisms.cost: Negligible.

mechanisms.name: Independence audit
mechanisms.what: Clusters notes three ways (union-find): same canonical URL, same wire-marker signature (marker plus the first 10 tokens of the first 1,500 characters), or exact Jaccard of 0.7 or more on word 3-shingles. The root (earliest created) scores 1.0; every other member scores 1/k. The step-3 orchestrator is told to add up these scores against a 3.0 consensus bar.
mechanisms.why: The idea is right: copies should not multiply consensus. But a k-copy cluster sums to 1+(k-1)/k voices, wire signatures key on page chrome, the root follows fetch order, and the counting is left to the LLM.
mechanisms.cost: O(n^2) pure Python: 0.6 s, 2.8 s and 17.5 s for 100, 200 and 400 notes of 1,500 words (probe); one CLI call.

mechanisms.name: Similarity primitives (shingles, Jaccard, MinHash/LSH)
mechanisms.what: Word n-gram shingles and exact Jaccard, used by the independence audit. A 128-permutation SHA-256 MinHash and LSH banding, used only by `hpr dedup`.
mechanisms.why: Infrastructure only. MinHash is not on the independence path, despite what the docs say.
mechanisms.cost: MinHash takes 0.45 s per 5,000-word document, about 2.3 minutes per 300 documents (probe).

mechanisms.name: Untrusted-content fence
mechanisms.what: Wraps the bodies of http(s)-sourced, non-summary notes in <untrusted-source url=...> tags with a treat-as-data preamble. Neutralizes forged fence tags (any case or inner whitespace) and HTML-escapes the URL. Applied in `note show` and `search`; the policy is also repeated in four agent prompts.
mechanisms.why: Lowers the chance that injected page text steers agents on the main read paths. But it relies on model compliance, covers only some read paths, and homoglyph or zero-width closers pass through (probe).
mechanisms.cost: About 70 tokens per wrapped body; negligible CPU.

mechanisms.name: Wiki-link parsing hardening
mechanisms.what: A linear-time wiki-link regex that rejects markdown-link labels, a CommonMark-aware linear code stripper, and a target filter that rejects footnotes, figure references, templates, shell fragments and path traversal.
mechanisms.why: Keeps junk links and stub notes out of the graph and avoids catastrophic regex backtracking on hostile bodies; the effect on reports is indirect. Cite-check uses only WIKI_LINK_RE.
mechanisms.cost: Negligible.

mechanisms.name: PageRank centrality
mechanisms.what: Power-iteration PageRank (damping 0.85, at most 50 iterations) over all resolved links in the whole vault, excluding stub notes, normalized by the maximum into notes.centrality_score.
mechanisms.why: Breadcrumb edges run from the fetched note to the note that suggested it (fetch.py:463-478), so suggesters gain rank, not the primaries several sources converged on (probe). It is computed vault-wide across unrelated runs, and carries only 0.20 weight in a composite that itself has little effect.
mechanisms.cost: Seconds of pure Python; one CLI call in step 2.

mechanisms.name: Quality composite and ranked search
mechanisms.what: A renormalized weighted mean of tier (0.35), utility/18 (0.20), citation authority (0.25) and centrality (0.20), with retracted sources floored at 0.05. `search --ranked` multiplies the BM25 score by (0.5 + quality) after the SQL LIMIT. Step 10 uses it to choose reading lists.
mechanisms.why: The retraction floor is a real demotion (x0.55). Otherwise multipliers range only about 1.10-1.20 and only reorder the top-N: a ground-truth primary beats a commentary hub by about 4% (probe).
mechanisms.cost: Negligible.
